html:
The Uzbek cotton scandal was a vast fraud uncovered in Soviet Uzbekistan from 1983, in which officials reported cotton that was never grown and shared out the money paid for it, by some estimates billions of roubles.

Under Sharof Rashidov, party boss of Uzbekistan from 1959 to 1983, Moscow demanded ever higher cotton quotas. Officials met them on paper by inflating the figures, and the payments for phantom cotton flowed up through a chain of bribes that reached Moscow, including Brezhnev's son-in-law Yuri Churbanov. After Brezhnev died, his successor Yuri Andropov launched an inquiry; Rashidov died in 1983 as it began.

Investigators opened some 800 cases, and more than 4,000 people were convicted. Churbanov got twelve years. Many Uzbeks saw the purge as an attack on their nation, and in the late 1980s the investigators themselves were accused of abuses and some verdicts were overturned. The affair fed both Gorbachev's campaign against corruption and Uzbek resentment of Moscow. It grew out of the single crop economy built by schemes like the Hungry Steppe irrigation, which also drained the Aral Sea.
sum: The Uzbek cotton scandal was a vast fraud uncovered in Soviet Uzbekistan from 1983, in which officials reported cotton that was never grown and shared out the money paid for it, by some estimates billions of roubles.
